content:
Mt Kenya hiking usually means a 4-5 day trek to Point Lenana (4,985 m), the mountain's non-technical trekking summit. Most hikers use the Sirimon, Naro Moru or Chogoria routes, climb in the drier months of January-February or July-September, and go with a licensed guide. Fit beginners can do it with preparation.

Mt Kenya is Africa's second-highest mountain, and planning a climb raises a lot of questions: which route, how many days, when to go, how cold it gets, how hard it is and what to pack. This complete guide answers them in order, with route stages, a sample itinerary, altitude advice and links to our detailed gear guides, so you can plan your climb from Nairobi with confidence.

Quick Facts: Mt Kenya Hiking

  • Trekking summit: Point Lenana, 4,985 m; the main peaks Batian (5,199 m) and Nelion (5,188 m) are technical rock and ice climbs
  • Main routes: Sirimon (north-west), Naro Moru (west) and Chogoria (east)
  • Typical duration: 4-5 days, often up one route and down another
  • Best months: January-February and July-September; the long rains run roughly March-May and the short rains roughly October-December
  • Summit conditions: below freezing at dawn, with a summit start at about 2:00-3:00am
  • Protected area: Mt Kenya National Park, managed by Kenya Wildlife Service and a UNESCO World Heritage Site

Where Is Mt Kenya and How Do You Get There from Nairobi?

Mt Kenya stands in central Kenya, just south of the equator, roughly 150 km north-north-east of Nairobi as the crow flies. Climbers reach the route gates from the towns of Nanyuki, Naro Moru and Chogoria, usually a 3-5 hour drive from Nairobi depending on the route and traffic.

The mountain is an old, eroded volcano whose slopes spread across several counties, including Nyeri, Meru, Laikipia, Tharaka Nithi, Embu and Kirinyaga. The upper slopes form Mt Kenya National Park, while the forest below is a forest reserve. Kenya Wildlife Service manages the park, and you register at the park gate before you start.

Most organised Mt Kenya hiking trips include transport from Nairobi. If you travel independently, matatus and shuttles run from Nairobi to Nanyuki and Naro Moru along the Nyeri side, and to Chogoria along the Embu-Meru road, but you will still need a vehicle for the final stretch to the gate.

Which Mt Kenya Hiking Route Should You Choose?

Choose Sirimon for the most gradual climb and better acclimatisation, Naro Moru for the shortest and steepest approach, and Chogoria for the most dramatic scenery. Many climbers combine two, such as up Sirimon and down Chogoria, to see more of the mountain.

RouteSide and start townKey camps (approx. altitude)Character
SirimonNorth-west, near NanyukiOld Moses (about 3,300 m), Shipton's Camp (about 4,200 m)Gradual, drier side, good for acclimatisation
Naro MoruWest, near Naro Moru townMet Station (about 3,050 m), Mackinder's Camp (about 4,200 m)Shortest and steepest, with the boggy "vertical bog" section
ChogoriaEast, near Chogoria townRoad head (about 3,000 m), Hall Tarns or Minto's area (about 4,300 m)Most scenic, with Gorges Valley and Lake Michaelson; wetter side

Sirimon route

The Sirimon route, the most popular choice for Mt Kenya hiking, starts on the drier north-western side, near Nanyuki. The path climbs steadily through forest and moorland to Old Moses Camp, then follows a valley up to Shipton's Camp below the main peaks. The gentle gradient gives your body more time to adjust to altitude, which is why many first-timers choose it.

Naro Moru route

The Naro Moru route is the most direct line to Point Lenana and is often done in three to four days. Above the Met Station, the trail crosses the notoriously wet, tussocky ground known as the vertical bog before reaching the Teleki Valley and Mackinder's Camp. The quick height gain makes acclimatisation harder.

Chogoria route

The Chogoria route climbs the eastern side through forest and bamboo to open moorland with views over the Gorges Valley, Lake Michaelson and the Hall Tarns. It is widely considered the most beautiful Mt Kenya hiking route, but it is wetter, and the road to the start can be rough in the rains.

What Does a Typical Mt Kenya Hiking Itinerary Look Like?

A typical Mt Kenya hiking itinerary takes four days: two days climbing to a high camp at about 4,200 m, a pre-dawn summit push to Point Lenana on day three, and a descent on day three and four. Adding a fifth day for acclimatisation makes the climb safer and more enjoyable.

Here is a sample four-day itinerary on the Sirimon route. Times are approximate and depend on your pace, the weather and your guide's plan.

  1. Day 1, Sirimon Gate to Old Moses Camp: register at the gate (about 2,650 m) and walk roughly 9 km through forest to Old Moses (about 3,300 m), usually in 3-4 hours.
  2. Day 2, Old Moses to Shipton's Camp: cross the moorland to Shipton's Camp (about 4,200 m), a long day of roughly 6-7 hours with the main peaks in view.
  3. Day 3, Summit night: leave at about 2:00-3:00am, climb to Point Lenana (4,985 m) for sunrise, then descend to a lower camp.
  4. Day 4, Descent: walk down to the gate and transfer back to Nanyuki or Nairobi.

A five-day version usually adds a night at an intermediate camp or an acclimatisation walk around Shipton's. Operators also run traverses, for example up Sirimon and down Chogoria or Naro Moru, which add variety without much extra time.

When Is the Best Time for Mt Kenya Hiking?

The best time for Mt Kenya hiking is during the drier months of January-February and July-September. The long rains (roughly March-May) and short rains (roughly October-December) bring more mud, mist and snow at altitude, and fewer clear summit views.

MonthsConditionsGood for climbing?
January-FebruaryDriest and clearest; cold, frosty nightsYes, peak season
March-MayLong rains; very muddy lower slopes, snow higher upPossible but hard
JuneRains easing, cool and often cloudyFair
July-SeptemberDry, cold, generally good visibilityYes, second peak season
October-DecemberShort rains; afternoon showers and mistPossible with good rain gear

Mt Kenya makes its own weather, so even in the best months for Mt Kenya hiking you should expect afternoon cloud and the occasional shower. Mornings are usually the clearest time of day, which is one reason summit pushes start before dawn.

How Hard Is Mt Kenya Hiking for Beginners?

Mt Kenya hiking to Point Lenana is non-technical, so fit beginners can reach the summit, but it is a hard trek. The challenge is the altitude, long days of 6-8 hours and a freezing, pre-dawn summit climb on loose scree and rock.

You do not need ropes or climbing experience for Mt Kenya hiking to Point Lenana, although the final section is steep and can be icy. The main peaks, Batian and Nelion, are a different matter: they are technical rock and ice climbs that need climbing skills, equipment and a specialist guide.

How do you avoid altitude sickness on Mt Kenya?

Avoid altitude sickness on Mt Kenya by ascending gradually, choosing a five-day itinerary, drinking plenty of water and walking slowly. Headache, nausea, dizziness and unusual tiredness are warning signs. If symptoms get worse, the treatment is to descend.

Altitude sickness can affect anyone, regardless of fitness, once you climb above about 2,500 m. The fast Naro Moru ascent gives the body less time to adjust than Sirimon, which is one reason five-day itineraries are popular. The NHS has a clear overview of altitude sickness symptoms and prevention, and you should speak to a doctor before the climb if you have any health concerns.

How should you train for Mt Kenya hiking?

Train for Mt Kenya hiking with regular long walks and hikes for at least six to eight weeks, building up to back-to-back days of 6+ hours with a loaded daypack. Hill climbs near Nairobi are ideal practice.

Good training hikes include the crater rim on our Mt Longonot hike guide, the long, muddy forest trail described in our Elephant Hill hike guide, and other routes from our list of the best day hikes near Nairobi. Use these hikes to break in your boots and test the layers you will wear for Mt Kenya hiking.

What Gear Do You Need for Mt Kenya Hiking?

Mt Kenya hiking gear centres on warm, dry layers: broken-in waterproof boots, wool socks, a base layer, fleece, insulated jacket, waterproof shell and rain pants, two pairs of gloves, a warm hat, a headlamp and water bottles. Add a warm sleeping bag if your operator does not provide one.

Our full what to pack for hiking Mt Kenya checklist lists 25 items, day by day. If you need to buy any of it, our guide to Mt Kenya gear in Nairobi explains how to choose each piece, and the Kilimanjaro gear checklist is useful if you plan to climb both mountains.

Which items matter most for Mt Kenya hiking?

The items that matter most for Mt Kenya hiking are the ones that protect you from cold and wet on summit night:

  • Boots: waterproof, ankle-supporting boots such as the Lowa Renegade Evo GTX Mid, broken in on day hikes first.
  • Socks: three or four pairs of merino wool hiking socks, with one dry pair kept for sleeping.
  • Gloves: thin liners plus insulated, waterproof gloves such as Thinsulate waterproof hiking gloves.
  • Light: a bright headlamp such as a waterproof rechargeable headlamp, plus a power bank kept warm in an inside pocket.
  • Insulation: a down or synthetic jacket for camp and the summit push.

Much of this kit can be bought as quality thrifted gear, which makes a full Mt Kenya hiking set far more affordable than buying everything new. You can try on boots, jackets and gloves at our Thika Road outdoor store at Mountain Mall, Nairobi.

Do You Need a Guide and Park Permits for Mt Kenya Hiking?

Yes, plan to climb Mt Kenya with a licensed guide or reputable operator, and pay park entry fees to Kenya Wildlife Service at the gate. Fees, camping charges and guide rules change, so confirm current details with KWS before you travel.

A guide knows the routes in mist, watches for altitude sickness and handles registration, while porters and cooks carry the heavy loads on most organised climbs. Kenya Wildlife Service publishes park information on its Mt Kenya National Park page, and you should check current fees there or with the park before you book.

What are the rules inside Mt Kenya National Park?

Mt Kenya National Park asks climbers to register at the gate, stay on marked routes, camp only at designated sites and carry out all rubbish. Kenya bans single-use plastic bags and similar items in protected areas, so use reusable bottles and dry bags instead.

Pro Tips for Mt Kenya Hiking

  • Go slowly: "pole pole" (slowly, slowly) is the best defence against altitude sickness
  • Drink early: sip water through the day rather than gulping it at camp
  • Pack dry: keep your sleeping bag and warm jacket in dry bags, even in the dry season
  • Warm batteries: carry your phone and headlamp batteries in an inside pocket on summit night
  • Pick five days: an extra day improves acclimatisation and your chance of a clear summit
  • Protect your skin: equatorial sun at altitude burns fast, so use sunscreen, lip balm and sunglasses

What Will You See on a Mt Kenya Hike?

On a Mt Kenya hike you pass through distinct vegetation zones: montane forest, a bamboo belt on some routes, open moorland with giant groundsels and lobelias, and a rocky alpine zone with glaciers and tarns below the jagged main peaks.

The forest on the lower slopes is home to wildlife such as monkeys, and animals including buffalo and elephants range through parts of it, so follow your guide's instructions. Higher up, the moorland plants, lakes and views across the Laikipia plateau and the Aberdares make Mt Kenya hiking very different from any day hike near Nairobi.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days does it take to hike Mt Kenya?

Hiking Mt Kenya to Point Lenana usually takes four to five days. Fast Naro Moru itineraries can be done in three days, but they give your body little time to adjust to altitude. A five-day trip on Sirimon or Chogoria improves acclimatisation and gives you a better chance of enjoying the summit.

Can a beginner climb Mt Kenya?

A fit beginner can climb Mt Kenya to Point Lenana because the route is non-technical and needs no ropes. Beginners should train for six to eight weeks, choose a five-day itinerary, hike with a licensed guide and bring proper cold-weather gear. Batian and Nelion are technical climbs and are not for beginners.

Which is the easiest route up Mt Kenya?

The Sirimon route is generally considered the easiest route up Mt Kenya because it climbs gradually on the drier north-western side and allows good acclimatisation. Naro Moru is shorter but steeper and crosses the boggy vertical bog. Chogoria is the most scenic but also wetter and longer to reach.

How cold is it at the top of Mt Kenya?

The top of Mt Kenya is below freezing at dawn, when most climbers reach Point Lenana, and wind makes it feel colder still. Nights at the high camps around 4,200 m are also around or below freezing. You need an insulated jacket, waterproof shell, warm hat and insulated gloves.

Is Mt Kenya harder than Kilimanjaro?

Mt Kenya's trekking summit, Point Lenana (4,985 m), is lower than Kilimanjaro's Uhuru Peak (5,895 m), so the altitude is less extreme. However, Mt Kenya routes are often wetter, boggier and more rugged underfoot, and itineraries are shorter. Many climbers find both demanding in different ways.

Final Thoughts

Mt Kenya hiking is a 4-5 day, non-technical trek to Point Lenana (4,985 m) that fit beginners can complete with the right preparation. Choose Sirimon for a gradual climb or Chogoria for scenery, go in January-February or July-September, take a licensed guide and pack for freezing summit mornings.
